metadata.title: The role of participation in training in the relationship between informal learning and its antecedents
metadata.venue: International Journal of Training and Development

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses secondary microdata from the OECD Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC) collected between 2011 and 2018, restricted to respondents who were working during data collection. The authors further construct a balanced cross-country sample by selecting 504 respondents per country (252 training participants and 252 nonparticipants) and aggregating across 34 countries (total n=17,136). The manuscript does not report the use of PIAAC complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight variance estimation; therefore, weight application cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Because the analysis is based on group mean comparisons and moderation effects using SPSS, the paper does not document any weighting-aware estimation strategy, which may affect generalizability under PIAAC’s clustered sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is Informal Learning Behaviours (ILBs) constructed from background questionnaire items (3 items) and analyzed via mean differences and moderation effects; the paper does not describe PV-based cognitive achievement scoring. Plausible Values handling is therefore not applicable to this outcome. For missing data, the authors explicitly state they excluded cases with missing data for the independent and dependent variables, so a PV/missing-data strategy is not required beyond listwise deletion.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used open PIAAC secondary data (collected 2011–2018) and selected respondents from 34 PIAAC countries in Europe, the Americas, and Asia who indicated they were working during data collection. Excluded all cases with missing data for the independent and dependent variables. To ensure a balanced training vs non-training comparison, limited country-size samples so that training and non-training groups had equal numbers; identified the country with the lowest number of training participants (n=252) and randomly selected an equal number of training or non-training participants from all countries, resulting in 504 participants per country (252 training, 252 non-training). Aggregated the country samples into a single dataset (n=17,136).

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (first cycle, 2011–2018) — adult background questionnaire (working respondents), aggregated across 34 countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Welch t-test: training participants ILBs M=3.54 (SD=0.982) vs nonparticipants M=3.12 (SD=1.124), t(16833)=25.91, p<0.001, d=0.396. Moderation: Participation×Readiness B=0.048, 95% CI [0.005, 0.090], p=0.028 (not significant per authors’ hypothesis test). Participation×Workplace Autonomy B=0.068, 95% CI [0.039, 0.096], p<0.001; simple slopes: with training B=0.088 (p<0.001) vs without training B=0.155 (p<0.001). Participation×Workplace Interaction B=0.108, 95% CI [0.081, 0.135], p<0.001; simple slopes: with training B=0.267 (p<0.001) vs without training B=0.375 (p<0.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC first-cycle (2011–2018) data aggregated across 34 countries for working adults, the study leveraged Participation in Training, Readiness to Learn, Workplace Autonomy, and Workplace Interaction to predict Informal Learning Behaviours (ILBs), finding that training participants reported higher ILBs (M=3.54 vs 3.12) and that Participation in Training moderated only the relationships between ILBs and situational antecedents (Workplace Autonomy and Workplace Interaction), with stronger associations among non-training participants. This indicates that workplace job design factors may be especially important for sustaining informal learning when formal training is absent, while training mainly shifts the level of ILBs rather than strengthening dispositional readiness effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses OECD PIAAC first-cycle secondary microdata (2011–2018) from 34 countries, restricting to adults who were working during data collection and excluding cases with missing values on the independent and dependent variables. The authors construct ILBs from three background-questionnaire items and model training participation as a dichotomous moderator, analyzing an aggregated dataset of n=17,136 (504 respondents per country; 252 training and 252 non-training). In the aggregated sample, training participants show higher ILBs (M=3.54, SD=0.982) than nonparticipants (M=3.12, SD=1.124), with a Welch t-test t(16833)=25.91, p<0.001 (d=0.396). Moderation results show Participation in Training does not significantly moderate the Readiness to Learn → ILBs relationship, but it does moderate the Workplace Autonomy and Workplace Interaction relationships (e.g., Participation×Autonomy B=0.068, p<0.001; Participation×Interaction B=0.108, p<0.001), with stronger slopes among non-training participants. Limitations include cross-sectional self-report measurement and no documented use of PIAAC complex survey weights in the provided text.
